old_digest: The side which bats first and leads by 75 runs shall have the option of requiring the other side to follow their innings.
new_digest: The side which bats firstand leads by 75 runs shall have the option of requiring the other side to follow their Innings

old_digest: One Wicket shall be pitched, as in Law G, with a Bowling Stump opposite to it, at a distance of twenty-two yards.
new_digest: One Wicket shall be pitched, as in Law 6, with a Bowling Stump opposite to it, at a distance of twenty-two yards.

old_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, Bounds shall be placed twenty-two yards each in a line from the oft and leg stump.
new_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, Bounds shall be placed twenty-two yards each in a line from the off and leg stump. 16

old_digest: The ball must be hit before the Bounds io entitle the Striker to a run, which run cannot he obtained unless he touch the bowling stump or crease in a line with his bat, or some part of his person, or go beyond them, and return to the popping crease.
new_digest: The ball must be hit before the Bounds to entitle the Striker to a run, which run cannot be obtained unless he touch the bowling stump or crease in a line with his bat, or some part of his person, or go beyond them, and return to the popping crease.

old_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, neither Byes, Leg Byes, nor Overthrows shall be allowed, nor shall the Striker be caught out behind the wicket, nor stumped.
new_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, neither Byes. Leg Byes, nor Overthrows shall be allowed, nor shall the Striker be caught out behind the wicket, nor stumped.

old_digest: The Striker shall be entitled to three runs for lost hall, and the same number for ball wilfully stopped by a fieldsman otherwise than with any part of his person.
new_digest: The Striker shall be entitled to three runs for lost ball, and the same number for ball wilfully stopped by a fieldsman otherwise than with any part of his person.

old_digest: Notes on Law 11. /V howler may howl with both feet behind the bowling crease provided that one foot is within the return crease. I f a howler knock the wicket with is foot in delivering the ball and remove a bail, such net does not in itself justify an Umpire in calling “No Ball.” When part of the bowler’s foot is grounded on or outside the return crease the Umpire should call “ No Ball.” If he delivers with the heel raised off the ground and keeps that jwirt of the foot which is on the ground within the return crease the delivery is allowed as fair.
new_digest: A bowler may bowl with both feet behind the bowling crease provided that one foot is within the return crease. If a bowler knock the wicket with his foot in delivering the ball and remove a bail, such act does not in itself justify an Umpire in calling “No Ball.” When part of the bowler’s foot is grounded on or outside the return crease the Umpire should call “No Bail.” If he delivers with the heel raised off’the ground and keeps that part of the foot which is on the ground within the return crease the delivery is allowed as fair.

old_digest: When only one run has been made from a “Wide Ball” the batsmen do not cross over to the positions they were in before the rim was made. When a wide is called the ball does noton that account become “dead” and the batsman may be out stumped or run out.
new_digest: When only one run has been made from a “Wide Ball” the batsmen do not cross over to the positions they were in before the run was made. When a wide is called the ball does not on that account become “dead” and the batsman may be out stumped or run out.

old_digest: An over should always he finished, unless a wicket fall within two minutes of time (see Law 45), or unless there is a local rule extending the lime.
new_digest: An over should always be finished, unless a wicket fall within two minutes of time (see Law 45), or unless there is a local rule extending the time.

old_digest: The Laws of Cricket, dearly make a distinction between the wicket-keeper and the fieldsmen and between cases of “stumping” and “run out” (see Laws 23 and 28).
new_digest: The Laws of Cricket clearly make a distinction between the wicket-keeper and the fieldsmen and between cases of “stumping” and “run out’’(see Laws 23 and 28).

old_digest: If runs are made off a “No Ball,” although the runs are scored and not the “ No Ball,” the bowler is allowed another delivery. If one run is attempted and the batsman is run out the “ No Ball ” alone counts.
new_digest: If one run is attempted and the batsman is run out the “No Ball” alone counts If runs are made off a “No Ball,” although the runs are scored and not the “No Ball,” the bowler is allowed another delivery.

old_digest: Note on Law 18. lu 1911 an agreement was arrived at between the Counties that “Trial balls, if both batsmen are at the wickets, bo not allowed in First Class Matches.’ This arrangement was approved and adopted by the M.C.C.
new_digest: In 1911 an agreement was arrived at between the Counties that “Trial balls, if both batsmen are at the wickets, be not allowed in First Class Matches.’ This arrangement was approved and adopted by the M.C.C.

old_digest: The wicket shall be held to be “down,” when either of the bails is struck off, or If both balls be off, when a stump Is struck out of the ground.
new_digest: The wicket shall be held to be “down,” when either of the bails is struck off, or if both bails bo off, when a stump is struck out of the ground.

old_digest: An Umpire would be justified in giving a batsman out “Bowled” if a stump were bowled down, but the bails by some mischance remained in position.
new_digest: An Umpire would be justified in giving the striker out “Bowled” if a stump were bowled down, but the bails by some mischance remained in position. The striker would be out under this Law if any part of either bail is “struck off” (see Law 20) the top of the wicket.

old_digest: (See Notes on Law !J2.) When a fieldsman catches a hall and falls and the ball touches the ground, it is a question of fact for the Umpire to decide whether or not the catch was completed before the ball touched the ground. When a Batsman plays a hall on to the ground and in order to prevent it hitting the wicket, after touching the ground, he strikes it again and the ball is caught, the batsman is not out.
new_digest: (See Notes on Law 32.) When a fieldsman catches a ball and falls and the ball touches the ground, it is a question of fact for the Umpire to decide whether or not the catch was completed before the ball touched the ground. When a Batsman plays a ball on to the ground and in order to prevent it hitting the wicket, after touching the ground, he strikes it again and the ball is caught, the batsman is not out.

old_digest: Notes on Law 23 If the ball rebounds oft the pads or person of the wicket-keeper, without having first touched the bat or hand of the Striker, and the Striker is out of his ground the decision should be “Stumped,” and not. It would not be out if he were to knock the bails oft' with his foot, or with an arm or hand not holding the ball.
new_digest: Notes on Law 23 If the ball rebounds off the pads or person of the wicket-keeper, without having first touched the bat or hand oi the Striker, and the Striker is out of his ground the decision should be “Stumped,” and not “Run Out.” It would not be out if he were to knock the bails off with his foot or with an arm or hand not holding the ball.

old_digest: A Batsman may be out 1 b w, although the bowler is bowling round the wicket, if the case comes within this Law.
new_digest: A Batsman may be out lb w, although the bowler is bowling round the wicket, if the case comes within this Law.

old_digest: It is sometimes only possible for a bowler bowling round the wicket to obtain an 1 b w with a breaking ball.
new_digest: It is sometimes only possible for a bowler bowling round the wicket to obtain an l.b.w with a breaking ball.

old_digest: If in making a second stroke to keep a ball out of his wicket, the Striker hit down his wicket as above he would be out.
new_digest: (See Law 16, Note 3.) * If in making a second stroke to keep a ball out of his wicket, the Striker hit down his wicket as above he would be out.

old_digest: Or, if the ball be struck or be stopped by any part of his person, and he wilfully strike it again, except It be done for the purpose of guarding his wicket, which he may do with his bat, or any part of his person, except his hands 5—“Hit the ball twice.” The fact that a run is attempted may he evidence of the batsman’s intention to t ike advantage of the second stroke and the Umpire is entitled to regard it as such, but it is not conclusive. Tf the ball has been lawfully struck twice and an overthrow is made, the batsmen are entitled to the runs which follow. (Seo also Law 22, Note 3.) Either Batsman is
new_digest: Or, if the ball be struck or be stopped by any part of his person, and he wilfully strike it again, except it be done for the purpose of guarding his wicket, which he may do with his bat, or any part of his person, except his hands;—“Hit the ball twice.” The fact that a run is attempted may be evidence of the batsman’s intention to take advantage of the second stroke and the Umpire is entitled to regard it as such, but it is not conclusive. If the ball has been lawfully struck twice and an overthrow is made, the batsmen are entitled to the runs which follow. (See also Law 22, Note 3.)

old_digest: It would not be out if the striker hit the ball into the opposite wickets —the other batsman being out of his ground—unless the ball had been touched by a fieldsman after being hit and before striking the wickets.
new_digest: It would not be out if the striker hit the ball into the opposite wickets—the other batsman being out of his ground—unless the nail had been touched by a fieldsman after being hit and before striking the wickets.

old_digest: When a run has been made off a no-ball the no-ball should be scored although the ball has been caught. 12
new_digest: When a run has been made oft’ a no-ball the no-ball should be scored although the ball has been caught. 12

old_digest: If the Ball, whether struck with the bat or not, lodges in a Batsman’s Clothing, the ball shall become “Dead.” 9 A ball does not become “Dead” when the bails are off’ or the wickets struck down or because an unsuccessful appeal has been made to the Umpire.
new_digest: If the Ball, whether struck with the bat or not, lodges In a Batsman's Clothing, the ball shall become “Dead." A ball does not become “Dead” when the bails are of! or the wickets stnick down or because an unsuccessful appeal has been made to the Umpire.

old_digest: A ball can only become “Dead” under Laws 33a, 33b, 34, 35, 41 & 50, or on the call of a boundary hit.
new_digest: A ball can only become “Dead” under Laws 33a, 336, 34, 35, 41 & 50, or on the call of a boundary.

old_digest: A bowler may run a Batsman out, without having delivered the ball, in anyway authorized by the Laws, i.e. he may have passed the bowling crease in his run or may change the ball from one hand to the other before throwing at the wicket or knocking off’ the bails.
new_digest: A bowler may run a Batsman out, without having delivered the ball, in anyway authorized by the Laws. He may have passed the bowling crease in his run or may change the ball from one hand to the other before throwing at the wicket or knocking off the bails.

old_digest: It is well to remember that a side which loses a player’s services through illness or injury, brought about during a match, is entitled to a substitute, “it shall be allowed” whereas under other circumstances consent is necessary which must depend upon the courtesy of the opposing Captain.
new_digest: It iswcll to remember that a side which loses a player’s services through illness or injury, brought about during a match, is entitled to a substitute, “it shall be allowed” whereas under other circumstances consent isnecessaiy which must depend upon the courtesy of the opposing Captain.

old_digest: In case any substitute shall be allowed to run between wickets, the Striker may be run out if either he or his substitute be out of his ground.
new_digest: In case any substitute shall be allowed tc run between wickets, the Striker may bo run out if either he or his substitute be out of his ground.

old_digest: The intention of this Law is that the injured striker’s ground, when he has a substitute to run for him, is at the wicket keeper’s end. He himself can only be run out at that end as provided for in the latter part of the Law.
new_digest: The intention of this Law is that the injured striker’s ground, when he has a substitute to run for him, is at the wicket keeper’s end. lie himself can only be run out at that end as provided for in the latter part of the Law.

old_digest: The Ball shall weigh not less than five ounces and a half, nor more than five ounces and three-quarters, it shall measure not less than nine inches, nor more than nine inches and one-quarter in circumference.
new_digest: The Ball shall weigh not less than five ounces and a half, nor more than five ounces and three-quarters. It shall measure not less than nine inches, nor more than nine inches and one-quarter in circumference.

old_digest: If he shall take the ball for the purpose of stumping, before it has passed the wicket, or, if he shall incommode the Striker by any noise, or motion, or if any part of his person be over or before the wicket, the Striker shall not be out, excepting under Laws 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30. The Wicket-keeper shall stand behind the wicket. A Wicket-keeper may run a Batsman out by going in front of the Wicket (Law 28) the Umpire must decide from the facts, if the act is legal.
new_digest: The Wicket-keeper shall stand behind the wicket If he shall take the ball for the purpose of stumping, before it has passed the wicket, or, if he shall incommode the Striker by any noise, or motion, or If any part of his person be over or before the wicket, the Striker shall not be out, excepting under Laws 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30. A Wicket-keeper may run a Batsman out by going in front of the Wicket (Law 28). The Umpire must decide from the facts if the act is legal.

old_digest: N.B.—An appeal, “How’s that?”.covers all ways of being out (within the jurisdiction of the Umpire appealed to), unless a specific way of getting out is stated by the person asking.
new_digest: N.B.—An appeal, “Mow’s that?” covers all ways of being out (within the jurisdiction of the Umpire appealed to), unless a* specific way of getting out is stated by the person asking.

old_digest: The side which bats first and leads by 150 runs In a three days' match, or by 100 runs in a two days’ match, shall have the option of requiring the other side to follow their innings.
new_digest: The side which bats first and leads by 150 runs in a threedays’ match, or by 100 runs in a two days’ match, shall have the option of requiring the other side to follow their innings.

old_digest: Where there is no play on the first day of a three day match Laws 53 and 54 shall apply as if the match were a two day match, and if in a three day match there is no play on the first two days, Law 54 and Law ‘one day matches’ shall apply as if the match were a one day match. Where there is no play on the first day of a two-day match, Law ‘one day matches’ shall apply as if the match were a one-day match.
new_digest: Where there is no play on the first day of a three day match Laws 53 and 54 shall apply as if the match were a two day match, and if in a three day match there is no play on the first two days, Law 54 and Law 1 ‘ one day matches ’ shall apply as if the match were a one day match. Where there is no play on the first day of a two-day match, Law 54 and Law 1 ‘ one day matches’ shall apply as if the match were a one-day match.

old_digest: The batting side has a right to have the ground swept and rolled “for not more than 10 minutes” before the commencement of each innings and of each day’s play. It is the duty of the Captain to see that his side obtain this advantage, 'rhe ground in this law means “the pitch.”
new_digest: In week end starts the wicket may be mown on the Monday morning under the supervision of the Umpires. The batting side has a right to have the ground swept and rolled “for not more than 10 minutes” immediately before the commencement of each innings and of each day’s play. It is the duty of the Captain to see that his side obtain this advantage. The ground in this law means “ the pitch.”

old_digest: After the actual commencement of play the ground may be again protected when necessary and shall be protected every night during the continuation of a match, but the covering shall be removed each morning, if fine, at 7 o’clock a.m The covering must not protect a larger area than 18ft by 12ft at each end, and must not protect more than 3ft Gin in front of the popping crease.
new_digest: After the actual commencement of play the ground may be again protected when necessary and shall be protected every night during the continuation of a match, but the covering shall be removed each morning, if fine, at 7 o’clock a.m The covering must not protect a larger area than 18ft by 12ft at each end, and must not protect more than 3ft 6in in front of the popping crease.
